extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: The precise origins of Sonnim worship are difficult to pinpoint, but it likely emerged alongside the prevalence of smallpox in Korea. The mythology surrounding Sonnim is less about specific narratives and more about a set of beliefs and practices. Smallpox was seen as a visitation from the deity, and its severity was interpreted as a reflection of Sonnim's displeasure. Rituals aimed to appease Sonnim often involved offerings of food and prayers, as well as the observance of strict hygiene practices. Shamans played a crucial role in mediating between humans and Sonnim, performing ceremonies to diagnose the cause of the illness and prescribe appropriate remedies. The absence of concrete myths surrounding Sonnim underscores the deity's primarily functional role as an embodiment of disease, rather than a character in elaborate stories.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Sonnim's primary role was to embody and inflict smallpox. However, the deity also held the power to cure the disease or at least mitigate its effects if properly appeased. The significance of Sonnim lies in the deity's representation of a major threat to human life and well-being. The deity's worship reflected the anxieties and fears surrounding disease in pre-modern Korean society. Sonnim's existence also highlighted the importance of ritual and communal practices in coping with adversity. The rituals performed to appease Sonnim reinforced social bonds and provided a sense of control in the face of an unpredictable and deadly disease. The deity’s presence also emphasized the precariousness of life and the need to maintain harmony with the supernatural world.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Sonnim symbolizes the unpredictable and often devastating nature of disease. The deity's role as an 'uninvited guest' reflects the sudden and unwelcome arrival of illness. The act of propitiation symbolizes the human desire to exert control over forces beyond their understanding. The offerings and rituals performed to appease Sonnim can be interpreted as attempts to establish a relationship with the disease, transforming it from an enemy into a potentially benevolent force. The absence of a clear physical form for Sonnim may symbolize the invisible and insidious nature of disease itself. The deity's power to both inflict and cure smallpox represents the duality of nature, where the same force can bring both destruction and healing.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: With the eradication of smallpox, the worship of Sonnim has largely faded from Korean society. However, the deity's legacy continues to exist in cultural memory and historical records. The practices associated with Sonnim provide insights into the beliefs and anxieties surrounding disease in pre-modern Korea. The deity's influence can be seen in traditional medicine and hygiene practices, which often incorporated elements of ritual and superstition. While Sonnim is no longer actively worshipped, the deity serves as a reminder of the profound impact disease has had on human history and the complex ways in which societies have responded to the threat of illness. The story of Sonnim is a testament to human resilience and the enduring power of belief in the face of adversity.

habitat: Ubiquitous; believed to reside in the air and affect households
name: Sonnim
description: Sonnim, also referred to as Mama or Sonnimne, is a significant deity in Korean folk religion, embodying the dreaded disease of smallpox. The deity's name translates roughly to "guest," reflecting the belief that disease arrives uninvited. Unlike deities who are actively sought for blessings, Sonnim was primarily propitiated to appease the disease and mitigate its devastating effects. The worship of Sonnim was widespread in pre-modern Korea, reflecting the profound impact smallpox had on the population. Families would offer prayers, perform rituals, and observe strict taboos to avoid angering the deity. The role of Sonnim highlights the complex relationship between humans and disease, where fear and respect intertwined to shape religious practices. The deity's presence underscored the unpredictable nature of life and the constant threat of illness, influencing daily routines and social interactions within Korean communities.

cultural.modernLegacy: Sonnim's legacy remains in cultural memory, representing the historical impact of disease on Korean society. The deity serves as a reminder of the importance of public health and disease prevention.

subtitle: The Uninvited Guest of Disease
appearance: No definitive physical description exists, but Sonnim is often imagined as an invisible force or spirit. Representations, when present, are abstract symbols of the disease itself. Some accounts depict Sonnim as a child or a traveler.
